lead: Remote sensing reads the ground from a distance by measuring reflected sunlight. This unit follows that light from the sun, through the atmosphere, off the surface and into a sensor, then shows how the picture is read by eye and by computer. After it you can explain spectral signatures, choose a sensor, compute resolutions, interpret a photo and classify an image.
about: The unit moves in one line from physics to product. Chapter 6.1 sets up electromagnetic radiation and the spectrum, the raw material of every image. Chapter 6.2 follows that energy through the atmosphere and its interaction with the ground. Chapter 6.3 turns those interactions into spectral signatures for vegetation, soil and water. Chapter 6.4 covers the platforms and sensors that carry the measurement. Chapter 6.5 ties platform height and sensor design to the four resolutions, which decide what is visible. Chapter 6.6 uses those limits to read images by eye with tone, shape, pattern and association. Chapter 6.7 replaces the eye with arithmetic: stretching, filtering, ratios, and supervised or unsupervised classification, checked by an accuracy table.

chapters.idea: Every remote sensing measurement starts with electromagnetic energy, which behaves as a wave whose wavelength fixes its frequency and photon energy.
chapters.depth: Definition of remote sensing and its passive and active forms. Electromagnetic radiation as coupled electric and magnetic fields travelling at c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Wave parameters: wavelength λ (m or µm or nm) and frequency f (Hz), with c = f λ. Photon energy E = hf = hc/λ, h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, quoted in joules and in electron volts. The electromagnetic spectrum from gamma and X-rays through ultraviolet, visible (0.4–0.7 µm), near, short-wave and thermal infrared, microwave to radio, with the band names and typical wavelengths. Sources of EMR: the sun as a 5800 K blackbody peaking near 0.5 µm, and the earth's own thermal emission peaking near 10 µm. Radiometric terms: radiant energy (J), radiant flux (W), irradiance (W/m²), radiance (W m⁻² sr⁻¹). Keep the derivation of Planck's law as a statement of the shape only.

figure.aria: A curve falling steeply from about 12 eV at 0.1 micrometre to under 0.2 eV at 10 micrometres, showing that photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.

chapters.example: Green light has wavelength λ = 0.55 µm. Find its frequency and its photon energy in joules and in electron volts. Use c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. f = c/λ = 3 × 10⁸ ÷ 0.55 × 10⁻⁶ = 5.45 × 10¹⁴ Hz. E = hf = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5.45 × 10¹⁴ = 3.61 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. In electron volts, E = 3.61 × 10⁻¹⁹ ÷ 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.25 eV, which also equals 1.24 ÷ 0.55.
chapters.trap: Wavelength and frequency move in opposite directions. A longer wavelength means lower frequency and lower photon energy, so infrared photons are weaker than visible ones even though infrared feels hot on the skin.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for units, scale and the idea of a measurement; basic physics of waves.
chapters.leave: Refraction and optics of lenses to physics; the sensor hardware that detects the photons goes to chapter 6.4.

chapters.idea: Between the sun and the sensor, energy is scattered and absorbed by the atmosphere and selectively reflected, absorbed and transmitted by the target, so the sensor records radiance, not reflectance.
chapters.depth: Atmospheric effects on the path down and up: scattering (Rayleigh by molecules, ∝ 1/λ⁴, and why the sky is blue; Mie by aerosols of size near the wavelength; non-selective by dust and cloud) and absorption by water vapour, carbon dioxide, ozone and oxygen. Atmospheric windows where transmission is high: visible, 0.8–1.3 µm, 1.5–1.8 µm, 2.0–2.4 µm, 3.5–5.5 µm, 8–14 µm. Energy balance at the surface with the conservation law ρ + α + τ = 1 for reflectance, absorptance and transmittance; albedo as the wavelength-averaged reflectance. Specular (mirror, calm water) versus diffuse (rough) reflection. The link from measured radiance L to reflectance ρ for a Lambertian surface, ρ = π L / E, with E the incoming irradiance. Path radiance as haze added by the atmosphere. Mention only a few universities derive the full radiative transfer equation; keep it to the formula and its use.

figure.title: Energy path from sun to sensor
figure.aria: A vertical flow from the sun through the atmosphere to the ground, back up through the atmosphere and into the sensor, with irradiance entering and radiance leaving.

chapters.example: A flat field receives an irradiance E = 500 W/m² and the sensor above it measures a radiance L = 25 W m⁻² sr⁻¹. Treat the surface as Lambertian and find its reflectance. Reflectance ρ = π L / E = 3.1416 × 25 ÷ 500 = 0.157, that is 15.7 per cent. If the irradiance is halved to 250 W/m² and the field is unchanged, the radiance falls to 12.5 W m⁻² sr⁻¹, but the computed reflectance stays 15.7 per cent.
chapters.trap: Radiance and reflectance are not the same. Radiance changes with sun angle, season and haze; reflectance does not. Converting the digital number to reflectance before comparing two dates is the step students skip.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.1 for wavelength, irradiance and radiance.
chapters.leave: Atmospheric correction algorithms and software to chapter 6.7, where they appear as one preprocessing block.

chapters.idea: Each surface has a characteristic curve of reflectance against wavelength, called its spectral signature, and the differences between these curves make identification possible.
chapters.depth: Spectral reflectance curves over 0.4–2.5 µm for the three main covers. Vegetation: chlorophyll absorption in blue (0.45 µm) and red (0.67 µm), the small green peak near 0.55 µm, the steep rise across the red edge into a high near-infrared plateau (0.7–1.1 µm) caused by leaf cell structure, then water absorption bands near 1.4 and 1.9 µm. Soil: a smooth, slowly rising curve with no sharp features, its level set by moisture, organic matter, iron oxides and texture; dry sand brighter than wet clay. Water: high in blue, falling through the visible and very low in the near-infrared, so water bodies look dark there; turbidity and algae raise the visible reflectance. Snow: very high in visible, dropping in short-wave infrared. Introduce ratios: NDVI = (ρ_NIR − ρ_red)/(ρ_NIR + ρ_red), range −1 to +1, and mention other indices by name only. Add that a spectral library stores these curves for matching.

figure.aria: Three curves: vegetation dipping in red then jumping to a high plateau in the near-infrared, dry soil rising smoothly from 10 to 34 per cent, and water falling to almost zero beyond 0.75 micrometre.

chapters.example: A crop pixel has red reflectance 0.10 and near-infrared reflectance 0.50. A bare soil pixel nearby has red 0.24 and near-infrared 0.32. Compute NDVI for both and say which is vegetation. Crop: (0.50 − 0.10) ÷ (0.50 + 0.10) = 0.40 ÷ 0.60 = 0.67. Soil: (0.32 − 0.24) ÷ (0.32 + 0.24) = 0.08 ÷ 0.56 = 0.14. The crop is vegetation because a high near-infrared and a low red give a value near +1, while the soil stays low.
chapters.trap: The green peak is not where vegetation is brightest. Vegetation reflects far more in the near-infrared than in green, so a false-colour image shows crops in red, not green.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.2 for reflectance and the atmosphere's effect on it; chapter 6.1 for band wavelengths.
chapters.leave: Crop growth models and biophysical parameter retrieval beyond NDVI; GIS overlay of the resulting index map goes to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: A remote sensing system is a platform carrying a sensor, and the choice of orbit and of sensor geometry decides what the image looks like.
chapters.depth: Platform classes: ground-based (tripod, crane), airborne (aircraft, UAV) and spaceborne (satellite), with typical heights — UAV a few hundred metres, aircraft 1–10 km, satellites 400–36,000 km. Orbits: sun-synchronous near-polar (Landsat, Sentinel-2, Resourcesat) giving the same local solar time each pass; geostationary at about 35,786 km over the equator (INSAT, GOES) giving a continuous view of one hemisphere; inclination and repeat cycle. Sensor classification: passive (optical multi-spectral, thermal, microwave radiometer) and active ( radar such as SAR, and LiDAR). Imaging geometry: framing camera versus across-track whiskbroom scanner and along-track pushbroom scanner, with the linear array of detectors and the swath. Spectral bands of a typical multispectral sensor and the panchromatic band. Real Indian examples: Resourcesat and Cartosat series, RISAT for radar, INSAT for weather. Cross-refer to Unit 5 for UAV, GNSS and LiDAR hardware detail.

figure.aria: A two-branch tree: platform splits into ground, airborne and space, with space giving sun-synchronous and geostationary orbits; sensor splits into passive optical and thermal, and active SAR and LiDAR.

chapters.example: A pushbroom sensor flies at 600 km with a linear array of 6000 detectors and a swath of 60 km on the ground. Find the ground pixel size and the field of view of one detector. Pixel size = swath ÷ number of detectors = 60 km ÷ 6000 = 0.010 km = 10 m. The detector field of view is the pixel size divided by height = 10 m ÷ 600,000 m = 1.67 × 10⁻⁵ rad, that is 16.7 µrad. The same array flown at 300 km would give 5 m pixels.
chapters.trap: Whiskbroom and pushbroom are both scanners but differ in direction: whiskbroom sweeps across the track with a moving mirror, pushbroom uses a fixed line of detectors and relies on the satellite's motion along the track.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.1 for the spectrum, chapter 6.2 for atmospheric windows that decide which bands can be used.
chapters.leave: Orbit mechanics and Kepler's laws to physics; GNSS, total station and LiDAR field procedure to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Four resolutions — spatial, spectral, radiometric and temporal — describe the limits of an image, and each is bought at the cost of another.
chapters.depth: Spatial resolution as the ground pixel size or ground sampling distance, from the sensor height H and instantaneous field of view θ by GSD = H θ, plus the mixed pixel problem when a pixel spans two covers. Spectral resolution as the number and width of bands (panchromatic, multispectral, hyperspectral) and its role in separating similar covers. Radiometric resolution as the number of discrete levels, a sensor of n bits giving 2ⁿ levels: 8 bits = 256 levels with digital numbers 0–255; quantisation step = radiance range ÷ (2ⁿ − 1). Temporal resolution as the revisit or repeat cycle, with typical values by orbit type rather than by satellite name. The trade-offs: finer spatial resolution narrows the swath and lengthens revisit; more bands split the incoming energy per band. Mention that only a few universities teach the modulation transfer function and signal-to-noise ratio as measures of real image quality.

figure.title: Same ground, two spatial resolutions (DN values)

chapters.example: Nine 10 m pixels in a block have digital numbers 10, 10, 10, 10, 70, 70, 10, 70, 70. Find the single digital number of the same block seen by a 30 m sensor and the fraction of the block that is bright. Mean = (10 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 70 + 70 + 10 + 70 + 70) ÷ 9 = 320 ÷ 9 = 35.6, rounded to 36. Four of the nine pixels are bright, so 4/9 = 44 per cent of the block is the bright cover, and the coarse pixel is a mixed pixel that belongs fully to neither class.
chapters.trap: Finer spatial resolution means a smaller ground pixel size, so the number 5 m is finer than 30 m. Higher radiometric resolution means more bits and more levels, not a bigger pixel.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.4 for platform height, swath and detector arrays.
chapters.leave: Resampling and pixel aggregation during correction to chapter 6.7; the raster cell model itself to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: Before any software, a trained eye identifies objects on an image by combining tone, shape, size, pattern, texture, shadow and association with the site.
chapters.depth: The elements of image interpretation, defined one by one: tone and colour (brightness or hue of the target in the recorded band), shape, size (judged against scale), pattern (arrangement of objects, such as an orchard grid), texture (frequency of tone change, smooth or rough), shadow (helps and misleads), site and association (what is normally found next to what). Interpretation keys: a written or pictorial table linking a land cover to its expected appearance. Image scale and its use: scale = photo distance ÷ ground distance, expressed as 1:50,000, and area scaling as the square of the scale factor. Types of image used: black-and-white panchromatic, true colour, false-colour infrared composite, thermal. Satellite versus aerial photographs, and the effect of season and sun angle on interpretation. Introduce visual comparison of multi-date images for change.

figure.title: From image elements to a mapped class
figure.aria: A downward chain where tone and colour, then shape and shadow, then pattern and texture, then site and association are pooled to produce an interpreted class on a map.

chapters.example: On an aerial photograph at scale 1:50,000, a forest patch measures 6.4 cm² and two field corners are 4.2 cm apart. Find the ground distance between the corners and the forest area. One centimetre on the photo represents 50,000 cm = 500 m on the ground. Ground distance = 4.2 × 500 = 2100 m = 2.1 km. One square centimetre represents 500 × 500 = 250,000 m² = 0.25 km², so the forest area = 6.4 × 0.25 = 1.6 km².
chapters.trap: Shadow can be read as a dark surface. A shadow also hides the ground it falls on, so a class inside a shadow must be confirmed from the sun-facing side or from another date.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for scales and map measurement; chapters 6.3 and 6.5 for signatures and pixel size.
chapters.leave: Photogrammetric measurement of height from stereo pairs and the plotting instruments; map projection of the finished map to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: Digital image processing turns raw digital numbers into a corrected, enhanced image and then into labelled classes, with an accuracy table to say how good the labels are.
chapters.depth: Image as an array of pixels with digital numbers. Preprocessing: radiometric correction (sensor calibration, sun angle, haze) and geometric correction with ground control points and resampling. Enhancement: histogram and its shape, contrast stretch (linear min–max, with the formula, and mention of histogram equalisation), spatial filtering with a kernel (low-pass smoothing, high-pass edge sharpening), and band combinations in a false-colour composite. Information extraction: band ratios, NDVI, and principal component analysis as a named method that only a few universities teach in full. Classification: supervised with training areas and the maximum likelihood rule, unsupervised with k-means clustering, and the difference between the two. Post-classification: filtering of isolated pixels, class labelling, and accuracy assessment with an error matrix giving overall accuracy and the kappa coefficient; state kappa's formula briefly as agreement after chance is removed.

figure.title: Digital image processing chain
figure.aria: A vertical chain from raw image through correction, enhancement and information extraction into a classifier, then a class map and accuracy assessment, with a dashed return to the classifier when accuracy is poor.

chapters.example: A band has digital numbers from 40 to 90 and is stretched linearly to the full 0–255 range. Write the stretch formula, then find the output for an input of 65 and for the two ends. Output = (input − 40) ÷ (90 − 40) × 255. For input 65: (65 − 40) ÷ 50 × 255 = 25 ÷ 50 × 255 = 127.5, rounded to 128. For input 40 the output is 0, and for input 90 it is 255. Every input below 40 would be clipped to 0.
chapters.trap: A high overall accuracy does not remove class confusion. Read the error matrix by row and column; a class can be 95 per cent correct on the diagonal and still have most of another class wrongly assigned to it.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 6.3, 6.5 and 6.6 for signatures, pixel size and the visual keys that become training classes.
chapters.leave: Spatial analysis and overlay of the class map inside a GIS to Unit 7; algorithms for PCA and clustering in depth to a course on pattern recognition.
